prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part for B042 naming Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. After reading the full first-round exchange, the case rests on the same points, and I am more confident in it because none of the six of us found a scientific weakness in it. The weaknesses raised are about credit. The discovery is specific and delimited. Human incretin physiology, the identification of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, and receptor and organ biology together established a mechanism that did not exist as a therapeutic concept. That mechanism has been confirmed independently for decades, including in large outcome trials with cardiovascular and renal endpoints. It is mature, and its effects reach several organ systems, which is the breadth the other shortlisted candidates do not match. I also hold to the view that the prize recognises a discovery and the change it brought to a field, not a product. A citation phrased around the physiology and the active peptide does that and still says plainly that treatment followed from it.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and I do not think round 1 resolved it. First, the Mojsov and Habener priority on the active peptide is something I know only from recollection, and all six of us said the same. A convergence of six recollections is not verification. Second, Knudsen is excluded by the cap, and I still regard that as a cost, not a clean exclusion. Extending the half-life of a peptide that is degraded within minutes was not routine, and a citation about physiology will read to some as under-crediting the step that delivered the therapy. Third, Habener's group is outside the credited names. If the committee cannot defend Mojsov's place in its written justification, my configuration should change to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen with a citation reworded around the therapy. I would not keep Mojsov by default, and I would not hold her place with a weaker argument just because the trio is tidy.

responses.point: The chair says the Habener gap is the hardest issue, that the committee should look at what Mojsov and Habener each did on proglucagon-derived peptides and the active form before settling wording, and that the citation should stay on physiology and the active peptide so it does not assert a priority we cannot adjudicate.
responses.response: I agree with the method and I would go further on one point. We cannot adjudicate the priority between them from the supplied record, so the question is whether the citation asserts more than we can support. My answer is that it should not say who first isolated or sequenced anything. The wording 'identification of its active form' credits a discovery step and leaves the order of priority unstated, and it is accurate for a group of discoverers. That keeps the text defensible, but it does not settle whether Mojsov belongs among the three names. That is a separate question, and the wording does not answer it. If the committee's honest conclusion is that her claim is not clearly distinguishable from Habener's, then the fix is to change the third name, not to soften the text. That is why I would state Knudsen as the pre-agreed fallback now, so that we do not argue it from scratch at the vote.

responses.point: Linnarsson moved from a trio including Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and states that if the committee finds the Mojsov priority does not hold up, Knudsen should replace her. He also notes that he accepted my point that Knudsen's engineering was not routine.
responses.response: I take that as a fair summary of where we both stand, and I think we now agree on the structure of the decision even if not on the odds. The trio stands if Mojsov's contribution to the active form is distinguishable and defensible, and Knudsen is the principled replacement if it is not. I would not, as I said in round 1, treat drug engineering as lesser in principle. My reason for preferring the trio is narrower and I want to state it plainly. The prize is for the discovery that created the mechanism, and the engineering depended on that mechanism existing. I would add one caution to your fallback. If Knudsen replaced Mojsov, the citation could no longer be written around the hormone and its active form. It would have to be written around the therapy, and that is a different prize with a different character. We should know that before we choose the fallback, not after.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius argues that attribution uncertainty should not push B042 below B038 or B013, whose credit lists have comparable gaps (Eshhar and Kuwana for CAR-T, Zhou for HPV), and that a two-part prize pairing GLP-1 with CAR-T or anti-TNF would force the GLP-1 credit below three names.
responses.response: I agree on the comparison. The gaps in B038 and B013 are at least as large as the one in B042 and they are less well known. For B038 the question is also whether the credit belongs to the receptor concept or to clinical translation, and Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer may be a separate achievement. So the uncertainty in B042 does not lower it. On the two-part question, which I raised in round 1, I now think your constraint decides it. With a three-person cap, a second part would force the incretin credit to one or two names, and every way of doing that excludes someone whose contribution is clearly discovery-level. I do not see a second achievement strong enough to justify that cost. I have therefore dropped the two-part configuration from my own thinking. I would say that to the chair as an answer to the question about defending a single part, and add that the committee should still say in its own records that CAR-T is the next candidate.

responses.point: Sandberg-Rickard asks what the single Nobel-level discovery in B041 is beyond clinical efficacy, and says a Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel configuration for B029 is defensible as a second choice though a tool is not equal to a discovery about physiology.
responses.response: On B041 I think your question exposes the real difficulty, and I do not have a convincing answer. Feldmann and Maini form a clean pair, but what they added to the already known cytokine biology was the demonstration of its role in rheumatoid arthritis and the clinical proof, and the antibody engineering involved many others. I raised B041 in round 1 as a possible second part and I now withdraw that suggestion for this year. On B029 I agree that the tool-versus-discovery question should be answered once. My answer is that the discovery that channelrhodopsin is a light-gated channel is a discovery, but the neuronal deployment is the larger part of the impact and it is a method. I still prefer B038 as the alternative because its clinical effect is demonstrated, and I note that the Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel set leaves out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck, which is a heavier fairness cost than any gap in B042.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is clearly distinguishable from the Habener group's work. I have not verified this against primary sources, and no other member has either. This is the one fact that could change my configuration.
If Mojsov is replaced by Knudsen, whether the citation can still be written honestly around the discovery, or whether it must shift to the therapy.

For B038, whether the prize should rest on the chimeric receptor concept or on clinical translation, and what to do about Eshhar and the separate adoptive cell transfer work. This affects how strong a fallback it is.

Whether durability of weight loss and long-term safety will alter how the incretin story is read in later years. I do not think it affects the physiology, but I cannot rule out effects on how the achievement is described.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict bearing on any shortlisted ballot. My earlier note stands: my Salk-era nuclear-receptor work with Ronald Evans and my dopamine-neuron research do not overlap with these candidates, and my past co-authorships with Svenningsson and El-Manira do not involve any shortlisted person. Nothing in round 1 changes this. The round-1 discussion has not raised any shortlisted person with whom I have a documented tie.
